title: The Quiet Month Trap: Why a Small Revenue Dip Costs More in Profit Than It Should
linkedin:
A business that drops ten percent in revenue this month can lose forty percent of its profit. Not because anything went wrong. Because of how the cost base underneath it is built.

Here is the maths, and why October is exactly the month to understand it.

Picture a business bringing in $100,000 a month, $60,000 of which covers costs that scale with volume (materials, subcontractors, job-based wages) and $30,000 covering costs that stay fixed no matter what trade looks like (rent, insurance, salaried staff, core subscriptions). That leaves $10,000 of profit.

Trade dips ten percent to $90,000. Variable costs fall with it, down to $54,000. The $30,000 fixed base does not move. Profit falls from $10,000 to $6,000, a forty percent drop driven by a ten percent dip in trade.

It runs the same way in reverse, which is exactly why a strong quarter feels disproportionately rewarding and a quiet one feels disproportionately painful.

Most owner-led businesses set staffing, stock and subscriptions to match the busiest quarter they just traded through, not the one sitting ahead. That is not a mistake. It is a normal lag, and it is exactly what makes profit swing harder than revenue does, in both directions.

The instinct when profit falls harder than expected is to cut costs immediately. Often the wrong move, because most of what moved was never variable in the first place.

A quick numbers note for October, especially if trade across Queensland, NSW or Victoria has settled into a quieter rhythm after the first quarter rush.

A small dip in revenue this month can take a much bigger bite out of profit than the percentage suggests it should, sometimes a forty percent fall in profit from only a ten percent dip in trade. This is not usually a sign that something has gone wrong. It comes down to cost structure. Costs that scale with trading volume fall when trade slows, but costs that stay the same regardless of volume, rent, insurance, salaries, core subscriptions, do not move with it. That fixed base simply eats a larger share of a smaller revenue number.

Most owner-led businesses set staffing, stock and subscriptions to match the busiest quarter they just traded through, not the quieter one that follows. It is a normal lag, not a mistake, and it is worth understanding before a quiet month arrives rather than during one.
